parts.label: a
parts.text: In projective space \(\mathbb{P}^3\), let \(V\) be a smooth quadric surface (degree 2) and \(W\) be a plane cubic curve (degree 3) intersecting properly (no common component). How many intersection points does \(V \cap W\) consist of, counted with multiplicity? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}\) defined by \(f(z)=z^{x}\). Determine the number of points in the target \(\mathbb{C}\) where the Jacobian determinant of \(f\) vanishes. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let \(Y = \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\) and define \(X = \{(w,t) \in \mathbb{C}^2 \mid w^{y+1}=t\}\) with the projection \(g:X\to Y\), \(g(w,t)=t\). Using monodromy transitivity, determine the cardinality of any geometric fiber of \(g\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

In \(\mathbb{P}^{3}\) a smooth quadric surface \(V\) has degree \(2\) and a plane cubic curve \(W\) has degree \(3\).  
Since they intersect properly and have no common component, Bézout’s theorem gives  

\[
\#(V\cap W)=\deg(V)\cdot\deg(W)=2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Thus the intersection consists of \(6\) points counted with multiplicity.

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=6\). The morphism \(f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}\) is \(f(z)=z^{6}\).  
Viewing \(f\) as a real map \(\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}\), its Jacobian determinant is  

\[
J_f(z)=|f'(z)|^{2}.
\]

Here \(f'(z)=6z^{5}\), so \(J_f(z)=0\) exactly when \(z=0\).  
The image of this critical point is \(f(0)=0\). Since the target set is \(\mathbb{C}\), the only point of the target where the Jacobian vanishes is \(0\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=1\). Then \(y+1=2\) and  

\[
X=\{(w,t)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\mid w^{2}=t\},\qquad 
g(w,t)=t,
\]

with \(Y=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}\).  

For any \(t\in Y\) (so \(t\neq0\)), the equation \(w^{2}=t\) has exactly two distinct solutions,
\(w=\sqrt{t}\) and \(w=-\sqrt{t}\). Hence each geometric fiber \(g^{-1}(t)\) contains two points.  
By monodromy transitivity the covering is connected, confirming the fiber size is constant.

\[
\boxed{2.0000}
\]

---

The plane cubic curve \(W\) lies in the same plane \(\Pi\) and has degree 3.  
Since \(V\) and \(W\) have no common component, Bézout’s theorem in the plane yields  

\[
\#(V\cap W)=\deg(C_{2})\cdot\deg(W)=2\cdot 3 = 6
\]

\]

\]

Hence there is exactly one point in the target \(\mathbb{C}\) where the Jacobian vanishes.

For any \(t\in Y\) (so \(t\neq 0\)), the equation \(w^{2}=t\) has exactly two distinct solutions in \(\mathbb{C}\) (the two square‑roots of \(t\)). By monodromy transitivity the geometric fiber size is constant, equal to this number.

parts.label: c

Assuming the geometric monodromy group acts transitively on the fiber over a geometric point, what is the cardinality of any geometric fiber of \(f\)? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For each prime \(p\) the map  

\[
f:\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p}),\qquad 
t\mapsto t^{5}+1
\]

sends every point of the domain to exactly one point of the codomain.  
Hence  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\bigl|f^{-1}(y)\bigr|
   =\bigl|\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\bigr| = p+1 .
\]

The average size of a fibre is therefore  

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1\qquad\text{for every }p .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

From part (a) we have \(x=1\).  
The morphism  

\[
g(u,v)=\bigl(u^{2}+v,\;uv\bigr)
\]

has Jacobian  

\[
J(u,v)=\det\begin{pmatrix}
2u & 1\\
v & u
\end{pmatrix}=2u^{2}-v .
\]

A point \((a,b)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\) is **bad** if the fibre \(g^{-1}(a,b)\) contains a point \((u,v)\) with \(J(u,v)=0\).  
The condition \(J=0\) gives \(v=2u^{2}\). Substituting into the defining equations of the fibre:

\[
\begin{cases}
u^{2}+2u^{2}=a \;\Longrightarrow\; a=3u^{2},\\[2pt]
u\cdot 2u^{2}=b \;\Longrightarrow\; b=2u^{3}.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus every bad target point is of the form \((3u^{2},\,2u^{3})\) for some \(u\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\).  
For odd primes \(p\neq 2,3\) the map \(u\mapsto (3u^{2},2u^{3})\) is injective, giving exactly \(p\) distinct bad points among the \(p^{2}\) possible \((a,b)\).

Hence  

\[
\frac{\#\text{bad points}}{p^{2}} =\frac{p}{p^{2}} =\frac{1}{p}\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}0,
\]

so the proportion of points where \(g\) is étale on the whole fibre tends to \(1\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=1\) be the limit found in part (b).  
Over the étale locus the geometric monodromy group acts transitively on each fibre, so every geometric fibre has the same cardinality, namely the degree of the morphism \(g\).

From the equations  

\[
\begin{cases}
v = a-u^{2},\\
u v = b,
\end{cases}
\]

we obtain a cubic for \(u\):

\[
u(a-u^{2}) = b \;\Longrightarrow\; u^{3}-a u + b =0 .
\]

A generic cubic has three distinct roots in the algebraic closure; each root determines a unique \(v\). Consequently the geometric fibre over any étale point consists of three points.

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\), a smooth conic (degree 2) and a smooth cubic curve (degree 3) intersect transversely (no common component). How many intersection points do they have, counted with multiplicity? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(f : \mathbb{A}^{1} \to \mathbb{A}^{1}\) given by \(f(t)=t^{2}-x\). Determine the value \(y\) in the target where the Jacobian determinant (the derivative) vanishes, i.e., the point that must be removed for \(f\) to be étale. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let \(g : X \to \mathbb{P}^{1}\!\setminus\!\{0,\infty\}\) be a finite étale cover of degree \(|y|\). Using the transitivity of the geometric monodromy group, what is the number of points in each geometric fiber of \(g\)? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the finite étale morphism f : \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Z}} \to \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Z}} given on affine charts by the polynomial map t \mapsto t^5 + 2t + 1. Compute the limit as p \to \infty of the average number of points in the fiber f^{-1}(y) for y \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Define the polynomial map g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2 by g(u,v) = (u^{x} + v, \; u v). Compute the Jacobian determinant of g at the point (1,2) and output its absolute value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Suppose we have a finite étale cover h : Z \to W of connected smooth varieties over an algebraically closed field, and that the geometric monodromy group of h acts transitively on the fiber over a chosen geometric point, which consists of exactly y points. Using this transitivity, determine the degree of the cover (i.e., the cardinality of any geometric fiber). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For the morphism \(f:\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb Z}\to\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb Z}\) given on the affine chart by  
\[
t\longmapsto t^{5}+2t+1,
\]
the reduction modulo a prime \(p\) gives a map  
\[
f_p:\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}).
\]

For any finite set map the average size of a fiber is  

\[
\frac{\#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}{\#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}=1 .
\]

Indeed,
\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}\#f_p^{-1}(y)
   =\#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p+1,
\]
so the average is \((p+1)/(p+1)=1\) for every prime \(p\).  
Hence the limit as \(p\to\infty\) is also \(1\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Here \(x\) is the answer from part (a), i.e. \(x=1\).  
The map  

\[
g(u,v)=\bigl(u^{x}+v,\;uv\bigr)=\bigl(u+v,\;uv\bigr)
\]

has Jacobian matrix  

\[
J(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u+v) & \frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u+v)\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(uv) & \frac{\partial}{\partial v}(uv)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1\\
v & u
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

At the point \((1,2)\) we obtain  

\[
J(1,2)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det J(1,2)=1\cdot1-1\cdot2=-1.
\]

The absolute value is \(|-1|=1\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

For a finite étale cover \(h:Z\to W\) with geometric monodromy acting transitively on a geometric fiber of size \(y\), the degree of the cover equals the cardinality of that fiber.  
Since the fiber contains exactly one point, the degree is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

For the morphism  

\[
f:\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb Z},\qquad 
t\mapsto t^{5}+2t+1 ,
\]

the degree of the map is the degree of the polynomial, namely \(5\).  
Because the morphism is *finite étale* it is separable and unramified, so over any algebraically closed field each geometric fibre contains exactly \(5\) points (counted without multiplicity).

Fix a prime \(p\) and look at the induced map on \(\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\):

\[
f_{p}: \mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}).
\]

Let  

\[
N_{p}=\frac{1}{|\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})|}\sum_{y\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}
\bigl|\,f_{p}^{-1}(y)\cap\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\,\bigr|
\]

be the average number of \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-rational points in a fibre.  
Counting the pairs \((x,y)\) with \(x\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\) and
\(y=f_{p}(x)\) in two ways gives

\[
\sum_{y}|f_{p}^{-1}(y)\cap\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})|
=|\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})|=p+1 .
\]

Since \(|\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})|=p+1\) as well, the average is

\[
N_{p}= \frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

Thus the limit as \(p\to\infty\) is simply  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}.
\]

\boxed{1.0000}.

Its dual curve \(D^{\vee}\) in the dual projective plane \((\mathbb{P}^2)^{\vee}\) is given by the equation \(a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = 0\) in dual coordinates \((a:b:c)\). For the line \(\ell\) with equation \(3x + 4y + 5z = 0\), compute the value of the dual equation at \((a,b,c) = (3,4,5)\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b

Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the binary quadratics
\[f(s,t) = s^2 + x\,s t + t^2\quad\text{and}\quad g(s,t) = 2 s^2 + 3 s t + 4 t^2.\]
Compute the resultant \(\operatorname{Res}_s(f,g)\) that eliminates the variable \(s\), then add 1 to the resultant. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Using generic smoothness, determine whether this morphism is flat over the point \(t = y\). Output 1 if it is flat and 0 otherwise. **Part (a)**  

For a given \(y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) the fibre of \(f\) is the set of solutions of  

\[
t^{2}+1 = y\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad t^{2}=y-1 .
\]

For a fixed \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) the equation \(t^{2}=a\) has  

* one solution if \(a=0\),  
* two solutions if \(a\) is a non‑zero quadratic residue,  
* no solution if \(a\) is a non‑residue.

Summing over all \(t\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) we count the total number of pairs \((t,a)\) with \(t^{2}=a\):
each \(t\) determines exactly one \(a=t^{2}\), so there are \(p\) such pairs.  
Hence the average fibre size over all \(a\) (equivalently over all \(y\)) is  

\[
N_{p}= \frac{p}{p}=1 .
\]

The map is étale away from the ramification point \(t=0\); removing the single
value \(y=1\) (the image of the ramification point) does not change the average,
so the limit remains \(1\).

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=1\) from part (a).  
For \(g(u,v)=(u^{2},v^{3})\) the Jacobian determinant is  

\[
J= \det\begin{pmatrix}
2u & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 3v^{2}
\end{pmatrix}=6uv^{2}.
\]

The morphism is finite étale exactly when \(J\neq0\), i.e. when \(u\neq0\) and
\(v\neq0\) (the factor \(6\) is invertible for all sufficiently large primes).

The number of points in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\) with both coordinates non‑zero is
\((p-1)^{2}\).  Hence  

\[
R_{p}= \frac{(p-1)^{2}}{p^{2}} =\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)^{2}\xrightarrow[p\to\infty]{}1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} R_{p}\times x = 1\cdot 1 = 1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=1\) from part (b).  
The morphism \(f(t)=t^{2}+1\) is a degree‑\(2\) map (the degree of the defining
polynomial).  By transitivity of the geometric monodromy group, each geometric
fibre has cardinality \(\deg(f)=2\).

Thus  

\[
\deg(f)\times y = 2 \times 1 = 2 .
\]

\[
\boxed{2.0000}
\]

The number of solutions is  

\[
\#f^{-1}(y)=1+\chi(y-1),
\]

where \(\chi\) is the Legendre symbol (with \(\chi(0)=0\)).

\[

      =\frac{1}{p}\bigl(p+0\bigr)=1 .

\[

The dual conic is defined by the inverse matrix \(Q^{-1}=Q\).  
A line \(\ell\) with coefficients \((a:b:c)\) is tangent to \(D\) iff  

\[

\]

With \((a:b:c)=(3:4:c)\),

\[

\[

\]

\(a_{2}t^{2}+a_{1}t+a_{0}\) and \(b_{2}t^{2}+b_{1}t+b_{0}\) is  

\[

+a_{2}a_{0}b_{1}^{2}-a_{1}^{2}b_{2}b_{0}
+a_{1}a_{0}b_{2}b_{1}-a_{0}^{2}b_{2}^{2}.
\]

\[

\operatorname{Res}&=1^{2}\! \cdot 5^{2}
-1\cdot5\cdot(-2)\cdot5
+1\cdot1\cdot(-2)^{2}
-5^{2}\cdot1\cdot5
+5\cdot1\cdot1\cdot(-2)
-1^{2}\cdot1^{2} \\[2pt]
